In October, the OSI hosted the State of the Source track at All Things Open designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. Duane O’Brien, Executive Director of the OSI, opened the track with “The State of the Open Source Initiative.”

The State of the Open Source Initiative

2026 has been an important year of transition for the Open Source Initiative, with a new Executive Director and multiple initiatives across Licensing, Policy, Standards, Open Source AI, and more. Duane O’Brien presented an overview of the OSI’s plans for 2027, and a readout on our mission, vision, and programs.

StateOSI Download

Video transcript

Duane O’Brien: All right, folks. Let’s go ahead and get started. Super appreciate you all making this your first post keynote session of All Things Open this year. And I’m apologizing in advance for a very beleaguered and tired me who got in at like 3:00 in the morning last night. So, welcome to the State of the Source.

This is the Open Source Initiative’s track here. We’ll be in this room all day talking about work that’s going on at the Open Source Initiative. You’ll hear from a number of staff members and myself as well. If you don’t know me, my name is Duane O’Brien. I am the executive director of the Open Source Initiative. I joined the organization in April this year. And so I’ve been on the ground now for about six months. Prior to my role at the Open Source Initiative, I was leader of an organization called collaborative engineering at Capital One. I was there for about two and a half years. That included the open source program office, the inner source program and a couple of other things. Prior to that, I built and led the open source program office at Indeed. I was there for about five and a half years. That organization also ran the inner source program and a hackathon and some other things. Prior to Indeed, I ran operations for PayPal’s open source program office for about three and a half years. And then I had a variety of roles where I was the Perl guy on the Java team in the industry. So, some kind of support engineering role, build engineering, performance testing, those kind of glue roles. If you go way back into the 90s, I was a play tester for Sony PlayStation games. So, if you ever played mid PS1 titles like Spyro the Dragon or MediEvil or Syphon Filter, my name is in very tiny print in some of those games. I started writing bugs for games and then started writing bugs for software and just sort of meandered through this strange history throughout the industry.

My intention today is to give you sort of an overview on the programs that we have at the Open Source Initiative. Some of our wins for 2026 and a little bit of a look ahead as we come into 2027. I want to start by really talking a little bit about our core mission because as we go out and talk about the work that the Open Source Initiative does, sometimes we blow past this point where we’re responsible for the licensing infrastructure for the internet, right?

There is a reason that when you go to an organization and say this is an open source license or this is an OSI-approved license, you have fewer conversations with your legal department than you do if you come in and say this license is bespoke or it’s been written by another organization because open source has a common shared understanding across the industry for what it means. And the Open Source Initiative is one of the reasons. We host the process to review licenses to see if they adhere to the Open Source Definition to protect user freedoms. We maintain the list of OSI-approved licenses. And we also host all the license text and protect the marks for open source in extremely rare cases.

So still when we look at open source OSI-approved licenses, we still get millions of hits a year. We get millions of impressions a month when you look at all of our license pages. And that reference to OSI-approved license appears in hundreds of places both in policy documents and guidance and in other references around the internet. That’s fun. So, we’re going to hope that my video comes back there, but I’ll just keep going.

Now open source licenses have been fairly stable for quite a long time. If you compare it to maybe 10 or 15 years ago, the volume of licenses at least until this year had somewhat trickled off, right? There were fewer licenses coming in. They were still very well understood. There was still a lot of discussion around it, but the recent slow proliferation of licenses that purport to address unique specific concerns related to open source AI has really re-energized this conversation.

And we’re having both some of a version of the same conversations that we’ve had for years about open source licenses, but some new ones as we’re trying to figure out how to come to terms with these new technologies that don’t look like traditional software. So that’s at the heart of what the OSI does is maintaining and sort of shepherding this license process. We very much see our role as the conveners of community and distillers of community consensus. Right? So the open source licenses aren’t what they are because the OSI said they are. Open source licenses are what they are because the community came together and defined these processes to say here’s what open source means and here’s what the open source licenses are and then we help to shepherd that process.

If you’re not familiar with the work that we do we have an entire group of policy folks that work with us through both the Open Policy Alliance and through a couple of staff members. I’m going to spend a little bit of time talking about US policy. Katie Steen-James, our US policy director, is in the room here and probably didn’t expect me to point her out. So a lot of what we do is we serve as subject matter experts to policy makers. We track both state and federal legislation when it comes to open source and open source AI. We lead the development of policy proposals for the Open Forum for AI, which is a partnership and collaboration run with Carnegie Mellon. And then we drive expertise into these channels so that legislators and policy makers can get access to guidance when they’re working on any policies or any proposals that might directly impact open source.

We do a lot of work with foundations to build coalitions of understanding with nonprofit foundations and organizations who need to respond to these specific kinds of concerns. And then we work to help make the case for philanthropic investment in this space as well and develop white papers that we share out with policy folks as well.

Over the course of the last year, the US policy team has chimed in on a number of issues. We’ve had a number of wins both at the state and federal level. From age attestation to the Open Forum for AI policy statement, there’s been a lot of discussion around open weights. There’s been a lot of discussion around AI transparency other places where we’ve chimed in to help make those bills better and in particular if you look at something like age attestation which was a requirement for operating systems to collect and produce you know some attestation about the age of the people involved, it requires some education with lawmakers to help them understand that open source operating systems do not work the same way as something like Windows and the creators of those systems follow a different set of rules. We help them understand those.

As you look ahead to the rest of this year and the next year, midterm elections are coming up and we’re not going to talk about politics, but we cannot get away from politics a little bit when we’re talking about US policy because how midterm elections go really sways the course of how those policy conversations are going to go over the course of the next year. So, we may see a lot more hearings in one direction or the other when it comes both to open source and to open source AI and to generative AI. So, we’re keeping an eye on that and we’re just sort of I like to tell people to stay on with the balls of your feet, right? You know, keep your knees bent and be ready to move in one direction or the other. And it’s also going to be really informative for, you know, what it’s going to look like in 2028 as elections continue. So, there’s a lot of work that we need to monitor there and geopolitical tensions continue to change and flow and that’s always a big factor as we’re looking at US policy.

As far as where we’ll be focused, these are some of the focus areas that we’ll have over the course of the next year. When it comes to procurement in particular, one of the things that we will want to see organizations do or want to see enforced sort of from the policy level is that open source solutions are considered along with proprietary solutions that come with a vendor, right? In many cases, the procurement processes in government organizations make it difficult to consider open source solutions because there’s requirements that come along with procurement that just aren’t there. So, we’re advocating for both an understanding of how to engage with open source solutions, but also to get them evaluated fairly against some of their proprietary alternatives.

When it comes to EU policy, our EU policy director is not with us, Jordan Maris. We had some great successes this year, from the G7 vision on openness, the EU tech sovereignty package, and then we’ve done some work around the CRA standards implementation that I’ll speak to briefly. The G7 vision on AI openness.

This happened I think it was May that it came in. So I was less than a month on the ground before this sort of came to a head. So it’s one of those things I got to take credit for but all I had to do was land the plane and I wasn’t even the pilot right like Jordan was the pilot on this one. So the French presidency of the G7 contacted us and they asked for support as they were working to develop a vision on AI openness. We responded we I get to say we a lot too. This with Jordan we responded you know attended a number of meetings in Paris between January and June. A lot of asynchronous work. We you know got a really positive reception from our collaborators and we this time we were invited to attend the ministerial meeting and then the dinner when they published the declaration. And so it was a really significant event. That really highlighted the OSI’s ability to go into rooms where sometimes not other organizations can because of the neutrality and the place that we sit in this ecosystem and engage with folks who are crafting really impactful policy.

The principles of the G7 vision on AI openness are that it’s community-driven, it’s not decreed from on high, and it comes out of the community that it’s measured to a variety of different elements and that it’s a spectrum but open source AI is a point on that spectrum and this has been a conversation that sometimes has been challenging for all of us to navigate when we look at something is it open source or not that’s kind of a fact but there are many stops on the journey to openness and so this articulation I think really helped that there is a spectrum of openness but open source AI is a point on that spectrum and that it should be described through appropriate labels and they landed on this set of four labels to help talk about openness with AI. There’s weights available, there’s open weights, there’s open source AI that is fairly conformant to the Open Source AI Definition that we published two years ago, and there’s open source AI with open data. So, not only is the technology open, but all of the data is open as well. So, this is the text that was in the G7 vision.

Now I was excited about getting to go over, attend this meeting, and sit at the table with the ministers. We’re going to play a little bit of game of magnify and enhance because those of you who’ve only ever seen me in conference wear are used
